opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, this is one of the things I find most exciting about the Virtual Lab setup, because it's something you just can't really do with human teams.

In a human research meeting, you get one shot. You gather everyone in a room for an hour, the discussion goes in whatever direction it goes, often shaped by who speaks first or who's most senior, and then that's the outcome. If you wanted to explore a different path, you'd have to schedule another meeting, and by then everyone's already anchored on the first conversation.

With the agents, we can run the same meeting many times in parallel. Same agenda, same set of agents (the PI agent, the domain scientist agents, the critic), but we let each run play out independently, often with a bit more randomness, so the discussions diverge. One meeting might focus on a particular modeling approach, another might go after a completely different strategy. Then we have a final merge meeting, where the PI agent looks across all those parallel transcripts and synthesizes the best ideas, catching things that appeared in only one or two runs.

That gives you a few advantages. First, breadth. You're sampling more of the space of possible ideas instead of getting locked into one trajectory. Second, robustness. If an idea comes up across many independent runs, that's a signal it's sound. If something appears only once, it might be a creative gem or a hallucination, and the merge step plus the critic agent help sort that out. Third, it's fast and cheap. These meetings take minutes and cost very little, so running five or ten in parallel is trivial compared with coordinating busy human experts.

It's a bit like having many versions of your lab exploring different parts of the idea space at once, then coming back together to compare notes. That turned out to be quite helpful when we were designing the nanobody pipeline, because the agents found combinations of tools and approaches that a single discussion might have missed.

And to be clear, the humans are still in the loop. We set the agenda and evaluate the outputs. But this kind of parallel exploration is a new capability that AI agents bring to how science gets done.

r001.rationale: The response says parallel runs use the same agenda and agents but diverge, with meetings pursuing different strategies.

r002.rationale: It describes exploring more of the idea space by running meetings in parallel, but does not explain that allocating more inference compute enables this exploration.

r003.rationale: It says the PI agent reviews all parallel transcripts and synthesizes the best ideas, conveying an overall synthesis across meeting logs.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this was one of the things that really surprised us. In the Virtual Lab, when we set up a meeting, we have the principal investigator agent and the specialist agents, say an immunologist, a computational biologist, a machine learning specialist, all discussing a problem together. And because they're agents, we can just run that same meeting many times in parallel. We'd run five, ten copies of the same meeting, each with a slightly different random seed, and then have the PI agent read through all of them and synthesize the best ideas.

You obviously can't do that with humans. If I have a lab meeting with my students, we have one meeting, we go down one path, and whatever we converge on is what we get. There's a lot of path dependence. Somebody says something early, and it anchors the whole discussion. With the parallel meetings, you get to see the distribution of where the conversation could go. Some meetings would converge on one modeling approach, others would propose something completely different, and the synthesis step lets you pull out the ideas that are robust across runs while also surfacing the creative outliers.

The second advantage is just the cost and speed. A meeting with the agents takes a few minutes and costs on the order of a dollar or less. So we could afford to iterate very quickly, run many rounds, and also build in things like a scientific critic agent whose whole job is to find flaws in what the others propose. In a human meeting, having a dedicated person whose job is to be critical the entire time is socially awkward. The agents don't have that problem. They don't get tired, they don't have egos about their ideas, and they don't mind being told they're wrong.

And the third thing I'd say is that the human expert's time gets used much more efficiently. In our nanobody project, the human researchers spent maybe one percent of the effort compared to what it would have taken to do this manually. Their job became setting up the agenda, reading the synthesized outputs, and making the key judgment calls, rather than sitting in every discussion. So the parallelism doesn't replace the human, it changes where the human attention goes.

r001.rationale: The response says repeated meetings can converge on different modeling approaches or propose different ideas.

r002.rationale: It describes running multiple meetings with different random seeds to explore possible paths, but does not say that allocating more inference compute enables that exploration.

r003.rationale: It says the PI agent reads the parallel meeting outputs and synthesizes the best ideas, including ideas robust across runs; this communicates synthesis across the meeting logs.

astra-6.text:
One advantage is that you can explore multiple directions in parallel. In a human research meeting, we typically follow one thread at a time, and the direction can depend a lot on who speaks first or who is most vocal. With the Virtual Lab, you can have several teams of agents discuss the same question independently, then bring their proposals together and compare the reasoning.

That also makes it easier to explore ideas that might otherwise get dropped. One meeting can focus on a particular approach, while another examines an alternative or tries to identify weaknesses. The value isn’t just having more discussion—it’s getting different perspectives that you can then synthesize into a better experiment. Of course, agreement among agents isn’t a substitute for evidence. You still need to test those ideas.

r001.rationale: It says independent teams can propose and compare different reasoning, but does not clearly state that the meetings can reach different decisions.

r002.rationale: It describes exploring multiple directions in parallel, but does not explain that allocating more inference compute enables that exploration.

r003.rationale: It describes bringing proposals together, but does not mention a professor agent synthesizing consensus across meeting logs.

sol-6.1.text:
One advantage is that we can explore multiple directions in parallel. In a human research meeting, we usually follow one thread at a time, and there’s only so much time for everyone to contribute. In the Virtual Lab, we can run several meetings with the same scientific question, let the agents develop different ideas, and then bring those ideas together for comparison and critique.

That also gives us a way to see which ideas are robust. Do different discussions converge on a similar approach, or do they reveal different assumptions and trade-offs? And we can ask an agent to play the role of a critical reviewer, explicitly looking for weaknesses in a proposal. So the benefit is both speed and a broader exploration of the possible approaches. Of course, agreement among agents doesn’t establish that something is scientifically correct—you still need to test the ideas.

r001.rationale: The response says parallel discussions may develop different ideas, assumptions, and trade-offs, but it does not clearly state that they can reach different decisions.

r002.rationale: It mentions speed and broader exploration, but does not explain that allocating more inference compute to parallel meetings enables exploration of more research paths.

r003.rationale: It says to bring ideas together for comparison and critique, but does not describe a professor agent synthesizing an overall consensus from parallel meeting logs.
